newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Rangebound, awaiting Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Rangebound, awaiting Greenspan.

text.p: U.S. credit markets will likely stay rangebound on Tuesday as players digest some fresh data and square portfolios ahead of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Wednesday.

"We've been rangebound for a long time and we're certainly going to stay that way until we get the Humphrey-Hawkings ... We might even stay that way after that as well," said Josh Feinman, global markets economist at B.T. Securities.
Greenspan will deliver the first leg of his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins speech on Wednesday. The second leg of Greenspan's testimony is scheduled for March 5.

On Tuesday, players will have mostly second-tier data to chew on, but experts said the numbers might move prices a bit. The day starts with the BTM-Schroders weekly chain store sales index for the week ended February 22 at 0900 EST/1400 GMT.

At 1000 EST/1500 GMT, the Conference Board will release the February consumer confidence report. Wall Street economists estimate the headline number will stay at 116.1 against 116.8 in the previous month.
The import and export prices report will also be issued at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
Later in the session, the market will take in Lynch, Jones & Ryan Inc's Redbook Retail Sales Index for the week of February 22. The data will be released at 1455 EST/1955 GMT.

"We do have some numbers. Nothing big, but we're going to get the weekly retail numbers and those have been running fairly strong for a couple of weeks now," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
"Consumer confidence is also stratospheric at this point ... There is some data that may move the market," Low added.

The U.S. Treasury market has been locked in a range for some time now because recent data stubbornly continue to show the economy is growing at a moderate pace, labor markets are tight, but there is no sign of inflation.
"Unemployment is as low as it is and inflation hasn't picked up," said Larry Dyer, government securities strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
"That said, it's difficult for the Fed to react until they have some reasons that would justify some kind of movement," the strategist added.
The Fed last changed monetary policy in January 1996, when it trimmed its target for its key federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.25 percent.
Analysts said large players and the buy-side of the market, which includes hedge, mutual and pension funds, have also been very slow lately.

Pundits said they noticed some fund buying over the last two weeks as those players extended durations on their portfolios. "But it looked like some of them sold a bit over the last two or three sessions ahead of Greenspan's testimony," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
The Fed added temporary reserves to the market on Monday through three-day fixed system repurchase agreements when funds were trading at 5.25 percent.

Analysts did not discount the posssibility of a coupon pass on Tuesday. But they said the Fed was more likely to carry out that operation on Wednesday, the last day of the current two-week bank maintanence period.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was quoted down 7/32 at 99-19/32 in late trading on Monday to quote 6.66 percent.
